lesson.tagline: Learning from examples that come with the answers 🔑

cards.title: Your inbox already does this
cards.body: Gmail learned **spam vs not spam** from millions of emails people had already marked. That's supervised learning: learn from examples that come with the right answer, then answer new ones yourself.

cards.title: In one line
cards.body: Inputs **with** answers go in → the model learns a rule → it predicts answers for inputs it has never seen.

cards.title: Studying with an answer key
cards.body: You try a question, check the key, and adjust. A model does the same thousands of times: guess, compare with the **label**, fix itself.

cards.title: How it works
cards.body: Every supervised project follows the same loop.
bullets: Collect examples: **features** (inputs) + **label** (the answer)
Split them: a **training set** to learn from, a **test set** to check
Train: the model tunes itself to make fewer mistakes
Evaluate on the test set it has never seen
Predict on brand-new data

cards.title: Two flavours
cards.body: What you predict decides the type of problem.
bullets: **Classification** → a category: spam or not, fraud or legit, cat or dog
**Regression** → a number: rent, delivery time, tomorrow's temperature

cards.title: The model is just a function
cards.body: Training searches for the f that makes ŷ as close to y as possible on the training examples.

cards.title: Memorising isn't learning
cards.body: Ace the training data but flop on new data? The model memorised noise: **overfitting**. Too simple to catch the pattern at all? **Underfitting**. You want the sweet spot in between.

cards.title: Myth vs fact
cards.body: The most common trap in interviews and in real projects.
cards.myth: Higher accuracy on the training data means a better model.
cards.fact: Only performance on data the model has never seen counts. 100% training accuracy is usually a red flag, not a win.

cards.title: What interviewers listen for
cards.body: Keep it crisp and show you know where it goes wrong.
bullets: A one-line definition plus a real example
Why you hold out a test set
Classification vs regression, with examples
Spotting overfitting from train vs test scores

cards.title: Recap
cards.body: You've got the core idea. Now go break the playground.
bullets: Supervised = learning from labelled examples
Train on one set, judge on another
Categories → classification, numbers → regression
Train vs test gap reveals overfitting

key_terms.meaning: An input the model uses, like hours studied.
The correct answer for an example.
Examples the model learns from.
Held-out examples used only to measure performance.
Great on training data, poor on new data.
Too simple: poor even on training data.

playground.title: Teach the machine 🎯
playground.intro: Each dot is a labelled example. The coloured background shows what the model (k-nearest neighbours) would predict anywhere on the map. Add points, change k, watch the boundary react.

tasks.prompt: Set k = 1, then add one orange point deep inside the blue area.
tasks.hint: Pick the orange class, then click on the map.
tasks.insight: With k = 1, a single odd point carves out its own island. The model memorises every example, noise included. That's overfitting.

tasks.prompt: Now slide k up to 15.
tasks.hint: Use the k slider.
tasks.insight: The island disappears. Each prediction is now a vote among 15 neighbours, so one noisy label can't flip it.

tasks.prompt: Push k to the maximum.
tasks.hint: Drag the slider all the way right.
tasks.insight: The boundary turns into mush and many points land on the wrong side. Too much smoothing = underfitting.

tasks.prompt: Drag the ⭐ point close to the boundary.
tasks.hint: Grab the star and move it.
tasks.insight: A k-NN prediction is just a vote among the closest labelled examples. Near the boundary the vote gets close, and that's where uncertainty lives.

tasks.prompt: Switch on test points and compare train vs test accuracy at k = 1 and k = 15.
tasks.hint: Use the 'Show test points' toggle.
tasks.insight: Training accuracy alone lies. A big gap between train and test accuracy is how you catch overfitting.

scenes.title: The answer key
scenes.narration: Every time you mark an email as spam, you're teaching a model. Supervised learning means learning from examples that already come with the right answer, the label. Show a model enough of them and it figures out the rule.
scenes.on_screen: Learn from examples that have answers

scenes.title: Features and labels
scenes.narration: Each example has features, the inputs, and a label, the answer. For a spam filter the features might be words and links in the email, and the label is spam or not spam. The model learns a function that maps features to labels.

scenes.title: Train, then test
scenes.narration: We split the data. The model learns from the training set, then we measure it on a test set it has never seen. Grading on the training data is like grading a student on the exact questions they practised: it tells you nothing.
scenes.on_screen: Never grade on the practice paper

scenes.title: Classification or regression
scenes.narration: If the answer is a category, like fraud or legit, it's classification. If it's a number, like rent or delivery time, it's regression. Same idea, different kind of output.

scenes.title: Memorising vs learning
scenes.narration: A model that is too flexible memorises noise and fails on new data. That's overfitting. One that is too simple misses the pattern entirely. That's underfitting. Comparing training and test scores tells you which one you have.

scenes.title: Interview takeaway
scenes.narration: In an interview: define supervised learning in one line with an example, explain why you hold out a test set, and show you can spot overfitting from the gap between train and test performance. That's the whole game.
scenes.on_screen: Define it, split it, check the gap

python.dataset: 400 synthetic app users with two behaviour scores and a label: subscribed (1) or not (0). The boundary between the groups is curved, generated with make_moons.

steps.title: Make labelled data
steps.explanation: Features X and labels y. Every row is one user and their answer.
steps.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# 400 app users described by two (scaled) behaviour scores.
# Label: 1 = subscribed, 0 = did not. The boundary between them is curved.
X, y = make_moons(n_samples=400, noise=0.35, random_state=0)
print("Users:", len(X), "| subscribed:", int(y.sum()), "| not:", int(len(y) - y.sum()))

steps.title: Hold out a test set
steps.explanation: 70% to learn from, 30% kept hidden for an honest score. stratify keeps the same class balance in both parts.
steps.code:
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42, stratify=y
)
print("Train:", len(X_train), "| Test:", len(X_test))

steps.title: Train and predict
steps.explanation: k-nearest neighbours predicts by letting the 15 closest training examples vote. fit learns, predict answers, score measures accuracy.
steps.code:
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

model = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=15)
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
new_user = [[0.5, 0.0]]
print("Prediction for a new user:", "subscribes" if model.predict(new_user)[0] else "does not")
print("Test accuracy:", round(model.score(X_test, y_test), 2))

steps.title: Spot over- and underfitting
steps.explanation: k = 1 memorises (perfect train, worse test). k = 151 is too smooth (both scores drop). The sweet spot sits in between.

mistakes: Measuring accuracy on the training data and calling it a result.
Splitting after scaling or feature selection, which leaks test information.
Forgetting stratify on imbalanced data, so the test set has too few of one class.
Picking k (or any setting) by looking at test scores; use a validation set instead.

questions.question: What is supervised learning? Give an example.
questions.answer: Learning a mapping from inputs to outputs using examples that already have the correct output (labels). The model learns from labelled training data and predicts labels for new data. Example: predicting whether an email is spam from emails that users have already marked as spam or not spam.
questions.interviewer_wants: A one-line definition, the word 'labelled', and a concrete example rather than a textbook phrase.

follow_ups.question: How is it different from unsupervised learning?
follow_ups.answer: Unsupervised learning has no labels; it finds structure such as clusters or lower-dimensional patterns in the inputs alone.

questions.question: What's the difference between classification and regression?
questions.answer: Classification predicts a category (spam/not spam, digit 0-9). Regression predicts a continuous number (price, temperature). Many algorithms come in both versions, e.g. decision tree classifier vs regressor. They also use different metrics: accuracy, precision, recall for classification; MSE, MAE, R² for regression.
questions.interviewer_wants: Category vs number, an example of each, and awareness that the evaluation metrics differ.

follow_ups.question: Is predicting a rating from 1 to 5 classification or regression?
follow_ups.answer: Either can work. Ordinal targets are often treated as regression (then rounded) or as classification; the choice depends on whether the distance between classes matters.

questions.question: Why do we split data into training and test sets?
questions.answer: To estimate how the model performs on data it has never seen. A model can memorise the training data, so its training score is optimistic. The test set acts as new data and must not influence training or model choices.
questions.interviewer_wants: The idea of generalisation and that the test set must stay untouched until the end.

follow_ups.question: What's a validation set for, then?
follow_ups.answer: For tuning hyperparameters and choosing between models. If you tune on the test set, its score is no longer an honest estimate.

questions.question: Your model has 99% training accuracy and 70% test accuracy. What's going on and what would you do?
questions.answer: That gap means overfitting: the model learned noise specific to the training data. Options: simplify the model (fewer parameters, shallower trees, larger k in k-NN), add regularisation, get more data, use cross-validation to tune complexity, remove leaky or noisy features, and for neural networks use dropout or early stopping.
questions.interviewer_wants: Naming overfitting from the train/test gap, then several concrete fixes rather than one.

follow_ups.question: What would low training and low test accuracy suggest?
follow_ups.answer: Underfitting: the model is too simple or the features don't carry enough signal. Try a more flexible model or better features.

questions.question: Explain the bias-variance tradeoff.
questions.answer: Prediction error can be split into bias (error from overly simple assumptions), variance (error from sensitivity to the particular training sample) and irreducible noise. Simple models have high bias and low variance; very flexible models have low bias and high variance. Good models balance the two, which is what tuning complexity and regularisation do.
questions.interviewer_wants: Bias = underfitting, variance = overfitting, and that reducing one usually increases the other.

follow_ups.question: How does k in k-NN affect bias and variance?
follow_ups.answer: Small k: low bias, high variance (jagged boundary). Large k: higher bias, lower variance (smooth boundary).

questions.question: How would you train and evaluate a classifier in scikit-learn?
questions.answer: Split with train_test_split (stratify for classification), create the model, call fit(X_train, y_train), then evaluate with predict or score on X_test. Put preprocessing such as scaling inside a Pipeline so it is fitted only on the training data. Use cross_val_score or GridSearchCV for tuning.
questions.interviewer_wants: fit/predict/score, a stratified split, and fitting preprocessing only on training data.

questions.question: Only 1% of transactions are fraud. Your classifier is 99% accurate. Is it good?
questions.answer: Not necessarily: predicting 'not fraud' for everything already gives 99%. With imbalanced classes, look at precision, recall, F1 and the precision-recall curve, plus the cost of each error type. Fixes include class weights, resampling, threshold tuning and stratified splits.
questions.interviewer_wants: Recognising the accuracy paradox and switching to metrics and thresholds that match the business cost.

follow_ups.question: Which matters more here, precision or recall?
follow_ups.answer: Usually recall (catch fraud), balanced against precision so investigators aren't flooded with false alarms. It depends on the costs.

questions.question: What is data leakage and how can it creep into a supervised pipeline?
questions.answer: Leakage is when information that wouldn't be available at prediction time reaches training, inflating scores. Common causes: scaling or imputing on the full dataset before splitting, features computed from the target or from the future, and duplicate rows across train and test. Prevent it by splitting first, fitting preprocessing inside a pipeline, and respecting time order.
questions.interviewer_wants: A clear definition and at least two realistic leakage sources with how to prevent them.

takeaways: Supervised learning learns from labelled examples to predict labels for new data.
Category → classification; number → regression.
Judge models only on data they haven't seen; tune on validation, report on test.
A large train/test gap means overfitting; low scores on both mean underfitting.
With imbalanced classes, accuracy alone is misleading.

A person watches the model while it trains
The model is retrained every day
questions.explanation: Supervised means each training example includes its label, so the model can compare its guess with the right answer.

questions.explanation: The test set stands in for future, unseen data, so its score is an honest estimate.

questions.prompt: What does this print's number tell you?
options: Accuracy on the held-out test data
The number of correct labels in y_test
questions.explanation: For classifiers, score returns accuracy on the data you pass in, here the test set.

questions.prompt: 1% of emails are spam. A model that says 'not spam' for every email has what accuracy?
questions.explanation: It's right on all 99% non-spam emails. That's why accuracy misleads on imbalanced data.

lesson.tagline: No answer key? Find the patterns anyway 🧩

cards.title: How does Spotify know your vibe?
cards.body: Nobody labelled your songs 'late-night lo-fi'. The app groups songs and listeners that behave alike, all on its own. That's **unsupervised learning**.

cards.title: In one line
cards.body: Only inputs, **no labels** → the model discovers structure: groups, patterns, or a simpler way to describe the data.

cards.title: Sorting a messy drawer
cards.body: No one tells you the categories, yet you naturally make piles: socks here, chargers there. Clustering does the same with data points that sit close together.

cards.title: What it's used for
cards.body: Three jobs come up again and again.
bullets: **Clustering**: customer segments, similar songs, topic groups
**Dimensionality reduction** (PCA): squash 100 features into a few that matter
**Anomaly detection**: flag the transaction that fits no pattern

cards.title: K-means in 4 moves
cards.body: The most asked-about clustering algorithm repeats two simple steps.
bullets: Pick k and drop k centroids (k-means++ spreads them out smartly)
**Assign**: every point joins its nearest centroid
**Update**: move each centroid to the average of its points
Repeat until nothing changes

cards.title: What k-means minimises
cards.body: Inertia: the total squared distance from each point to its own centroid. Smaller means tighter clusters.

symbols.meaning: the centroid of the cluster xᵢ belongs to

cards.title: So how many clusters?
cards.body: Inertia always drops as k grows, so don't just minimise it. Look for the **elbow** where gains flatten, and check the **silhouette** score (closer to 1 = better separated).

cards.title: Myth vs fact
cards.body: Clusters are a lens, not the truth.
cards.myth: The clusters k-means finds are the real, natural groups in the data.
cards.fact: K-means always returns k groups, even in random noise. It assumes round, similar-sized clusters, and it's sensitive to feature scaling.

cards.title: What interviewers listen for
cards.body: Show you know the algorithm and its limits.
bullets: Supervised vs unsupervised in one line
The assign → update loop of k-means
Choosing k: elbow + silhouette
Why you scale features first

cards.title: Recap
cards.body: Now go watch clusters form in the playground.
bullets: Unsupervised = no labels, find structure
K-means: assign to nearest centroid, move centroids, repeat
Pick k with the elbow and silhouette
Scale features; expect round clusters

key_terms.meaning: A group of points that are similar to each other.
The average point of a cluster.
Total squared distance of points to their centroid.
Pick k where adding clusters stops helping much.
From −1 to 1: how well separated clusters are.

playground.title: Watch clusters form 🫧
playground.intro: The points have no labels. Pick k, then step through k-means: points join their nearest centroid, centroids move to the middle of their group, repeat.

tasks.prompt: Keep k = 3 and press Step a few times.
tasks.hint: Each press does one assign or one update.
tasks.insight: Centroids slide toward the centre of their groups and stop once no point changes cluster. That's convergence.

tasks.prompt: Set k = 6 on data with 3 visible blobs.
tasks.hint: Move the k slider, then Run.
tasks.insight: K-means happily splits real groups to give you 6. It always returns exactly k clusters, whether or not they make sense.

tasks.prompt: Open the elbow chart and find where the curve bends.
tasks.hint: Look for where the line stops dropping steeply.
tasks.insight: Inertia always shrinks as k grows. The bend (the elbow) is where extra clusters stop buying much.

tasks.prompt: Press New starting points a few times with k = 4.
tasks.hint: Same data, different random centroids.
tasks.insight: Different starts can end in different answers. That's why libraries run k-means several times (n_init) and keep the best.

scenes.title: No answers given
scenes.narration: In supervised learning every example comes with an answer. Here there are none. Unsupervised learning looks only at the inputs and finds structure nobody pointed out, like groups of similar customers or songs.

scenes.title: Three big jobs
scenes.narration: Most unsupervised work is one of three jobs: clustering similar items, reducing many features to a few with methods like PCA, or spotting anomalies that fit no pattern, like a suspicious payment.

scenes.title: K-means, step by step
scenes.narration: K-means starts with k centroids. Each point joins the nearest one. Then every centroid moves to the average of its points. Assign, update, repeat, until nothing changes. Simple, fast, and everywhere.

scenes.title: What it optimises
scenes.narration: Behind the scenes, k-means minimises inertia: the total squared distance from each point to its centroid. Each assign step and each update step can only lower it, which is why the algorithm settles down.

scenes.title: Choosing k
scenes.narration: Inertia always falls as you add clusters, so you can't just minimise it. Plot it against k and look for the elbow, then check the silhouette score, which rewards tight, well separated clusters.

scenes.title: Interview takeaway
scenes.narration: Explain the assign and update loop, how you'd pick k, and the catches: scale your features, expect round clusters, and remember k-means returns k groups even when the data has none.
scenes.on_screen: Know the loop, know the limits

python.dataset: 300 synthetic shoppers with two features, generated with make_blobs. The true group labels exist but we deliberately throw them away.

steps.title: Unlabelled data
steps.explanation: make_blobs also returns labels; the underscore throws them away so the model only ever sees X.
steps.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs

# 300 shoppers described by two features. We never use the "true group" labels.
X, _ = make_blobs(n_samples=300, centers=3, cluster_std=0.9, random_state=7)
print("Shoppers:", X.shape[0], "| features:", X.shape[1])

steps.title: Run k-means
steps.explanation: n_init=10 runs ten different starts and keeps the best; random_state makes it repeatable.
steps.code:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=3, n_init=10, random_state=0)
labels = kmeans.fit_predict(X)
sizes = np.bincount(labels)
print("Cluster sizes:", sorted(sizes.tolist()))
print("Inertia (k=3):", round(kmeans.inertia_, 1))

steps.title: The elbow
steps.explanation: Inertia for k = 1…6. Watch the huge drops stop after k = 3.

steps.title: Silhouette check
steps.explanation: Higher is better separated. It peaks at the k the data supports.
steps.code:
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

for k in (2, 3, 4):
    labels_k = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(X)
    print(f"k={k}  silhouette={silhouette_score(X, labels_k):.2f}")

questions.question: What is unsupervised learning? How does it differ from supervised learning?
questions.answer: Unsupervised learning works with unlabelled data and finds structure in the inputs alone, such as clusters, lower-dimensional representations or anomalies. Supervised learning needs labels and learns to predict them. Example: segmenting customers by behaviour without any predefined segments.
questions.interviewer_wants: The 'no labels' point, a task type (clustering, reduction, anomaly detection) and a real example.

follow_ups.question: How do you evaluate a model when there are no labels?
follow_ups.answer: With internal metrics (inertia, silhouette), stability across runs, and whether the result is useful downstream or makes sense to domain experts.

questions.question: Walk me through the k-means algorithm.
questions.answer: Choose k and initialise k centroids (usually with k-means++). Repeat: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its assigned points. Stop when assignments no longer change or a maximum number of iterations is reached. It minimises the within-cluster sum of squared distances.
questions.interviewer_wants: The two alternating steps, the stopping condition, and what objective it minimises.

follow_ups.question: Is k-means guaranteed to find the best clustering?
follow_ups.answer: No. It converges to a local minimum that depends on initialisation, which is why it's run several times (n_init).

questions.question: How do you choose the number of clusters k?
questions.answer: Plot inertia against k and look for the elbow where improvements flatten; compute the silhouette score for several k and prefer higher values; use the gap statistic; and above all check whether the clusters are interpretable and useful for the business question.
questions.interviewer_wants: More than one method, and the note that inertia always decreases with k.

questions.question: One feature is annual income in rupees, another is age. You run k-means and the clusters only split by income. Why?
questions.answer: K-means uses Euclidean distance, and income's scale is far larger than age's, so it dominates every distance. Standardise or normalise features (e.g. StandardScaler) before clustering so each contributes fairly.
questions.interviewer_wants: Distance-based algorithms need feature scaling, and why.

questions.question: What does a silhouette score of 0.8 vs 0.1 tell you?
questions.answer: The silhouette compares each point's average distance to its own cluster (a) with its distance to the nearest other cluster (b): s = (b − a) / max(a, b). Near 1 means well separated clusters (0.8 is strong); near 0 means points sit on the borders between clusters (0.1 is weak); negative suggests misassignment.
questions.interviewer_wants: What the score compares, its range, and how to read values.

questions.question: When does k-means fail, and what would you use instead?
questions.answer: It assumes roughly spherical, similarly sized clusters, so it struggles with elongated or curved shapes, very different densities, and outliers (which drag centroids). Alternatives: DBSCAN or HDBSCAN for arbitrary shapes and noise, Gaussian Mixture Models for elliptical clusters with soft assignments, and hierarchical clustering when you want a dendrogram.
questions.interviewer_wants: Concrete failure cases and matching alternatives.

follow_ups.question: What does DBSCAN need instead of k?
follow_ups.answer: A neighbourhood radius (eps) and a minimum number of points; it finds dense regions and marks sparse points as noise.

questions.question: How would you cluster customers in scikit-learn so the result is reproducible and fair to every feature?
questions.answer: Build a Pipeline with StandardScaler followed by KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=0). Fit on the customer features, read labels_ or call predict for new customers, and evaluate k with inertia and silhouette_score.
questions.interviewer_wants: Scaling inside a pipeline, n_init, random_state, and an evaluation step.

takeaways: Unsupervised learning finds structure without labels.
K-means alternates assign and update steps to minimise inertia.
Choose k with the elbow, silhouette and common sense.
Scale features; k-means prefers round, similar-sized clusters.

cards.title: Guess the rent
cards.body: Bigger flat, higher rent. Roughly. **Linear regression** turns that 'roughly' into a line you can use: give it a size, get a predicted rent.

cards.title: In one line
cards.body: Fit the straight line that keeps the **squared errors** as small as possible, then use it to predict numbers.

python.dataset: 50 synthetic flats: size in m² and monthly rent in thousands of rupees, with random noise added to a true line (rent = 4 + 0.25 × size).

steps.title: Make the data
steps.explanation: A true line plus noise, with a fixed seed so everyone sees the same numbers.
steps.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
# 50 flats: size in square metres -> rent in thousands of rupees per month.
size = rng.uniform(30, 120, 50)
rent = 4 + 0.25 * size + rng.normal(0, 2.5, 50)
print("First 3 flats:", [(int(round(s)), float(round(r, 1))) for s, r in zip(size[:3], rent[:3])])

steps.title: Least squares by hand
steps.explanation: Slope = covariance / variance; the line passes through the mean point.
steps.code:
# Least squares by hand: slope = cov(x, y) / var(x)
w = np.sum((size - size.mean()) * (rent - rent.mean())) / np.sum((size - size.mean()) ** 2)
b = rent.mean() - w * size.mean()
print(f"By hand:       rent = {w:.3f} * size + {b:.2f}")

steps.title: Same thing with scikit-learn
steps.explanation: scikit-learn expects a 2-D feature array, hence reshape(-1, 1).
steps.code:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

model = LinearRegression().fit(size.reshape(-1, 1), rent)
print(f"scikit-learn:  rent = {model.coef_[0]:.3f} * size + {model.intercept_:.2f}")

steps.title: Evaluate and predict
steps.explanation: MSE is in squared units; R² is unit-free. Then predict an 80 m² flat.
steps.code:
predicted = model.predict(size.reshape(-1, 1))
mse = np.mean((rent - predicted) ** 2)
r2 = model.score(size.reshape(-1, 1), rent)
print(f"MSE = {mse:.2f}   R^2 = {r2:.3f}")
print(f"Predicted rent for 80 m^2: {model.predict([[80]])[0]:.1f}k")

questions.question: What is linear regression?
questions.answer: A supervised method that predicts a continuous target as a linear combination of the features: ŷ = w·x + b (or ŷ = Xw + b with many features). It learns the weights that minimise the mean squared error between predictions and true values.
questions.interviewer_wants: The equation, 'continuous target', and that it minimises squared error.

follow_ups.question: What does the slope mean in plain words?
follow_ups.answer: How much the prediction changes for a one-unit increase in that feature, holding other features fixed.

questions.question: Why do we minimise squared errors rather than plain errors?
questions.answer: Plain errors can cancel out (positive and negative), so their sum can be zero for a bad line. Squaring keeps every error positive, penalises large errors more, and gives a smooth, convex loss with a unique minimum and a closed-form solution.
questions.interviewer_wants: Cancellation, penalising big errors, and convexity.

follow_ups.question: What's a downside of squaring?
follow_ups.answer: Outliers get huge weight. Mean absolute error or Huber loss are more robust.

questions.question: What do MSE and R² tell you?
questions.answer: MSE is the average squared residual, in squared units of the target; lower is better. R² is the share of the target's variance the model explains: 1 is perfect, 0 is no better than predicting the mean, and it can be negative for a model worse than the mean.
questions.interviewer_wants: Correct interpretation of both, including R²'s baseline.

questions.question: Derive the slope of simple linear regression.
questions.answer: Minimise Σ(yᵢ − w·xᵢ − b)². Setting the derivative with respect to b to zero gives b = ȳ − w·x̄. Substituting and setting the derivative with respect to w to zero gives w = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / Σ(xᵢ − x̄)², i.e. cov(x, y) / var(x).
questions.interviewer_wants: Partial derivatives set to zero and the covariance over variance result.

follow_ups.question: What's the matrix form?
follow_ups.answer: w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy, the normal equation, with a column of ones for the intercept.

questions.question: What assumptions does linear regression make?
questions.answer: A linear relationship between features and target; independent errors; constant error variance (homoscedasticity); and, for confidence intervals and p-values, roughly normal errors. Strongly correlated features (multicollinearity) make individual coefficients unstable.
questions.interviewer_wants: Linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, normality for inference, and multicollinearity.

questions.question: When would you use gradient descent instead of the normal equation?
questions.answer: When there are many features (inverting XᵀX costs about O(d³)), very large datasets that don't fit in memory, or streaming data. Gradient descent and its stochastic variants scale; the normal equation is exact and fast for small problems.
questions.interviewer_wants: Computational cost reasoning, not just 'it's faster'.

questions.question: What are Ridge and Lasso, and when would you use them?
questions.answer: Both add a penalty to the loss to shrink weights and reduce overfitting. Ridge adds λΣw², shrinking all weights smoothly and helping with multicollinearity. Lasso adds λΣ|w|, which can drive some weights exactly to zero, doing feature selection. Elastic Net mixes both.
questions.interviewer_wants: L2 vs L1 penalties, shrinkage vs sparsity, and when each helps.

follow_ups.question: Why should features be scaled before regularising?
follow_ups.answer: The penalty treats all weights equally, so features on larger scales would be penalised unfairly.

questions.question: Your residual plot shows a curve. What does it mean and what do you do?
questions.answer: The relationship isn't linear in the current features, so the model is systematically wrong in parts of the range. Add polynomial or transformed features (e.g. log), or use a non-linear model such as gradient-boosted trees.
questions.interviewer_wants: Reading residual plots and fixing non-linearity.

takeaways: ŷ = w·x + b, fitted by minimising mean squared error.
Slope = cov(x, y) / var(x) for one feature.
MSE measures error; R² measures explained variance against the mean baseline.
Outliers, non-linearity and multicollinearity are the classic pitfalls.

python.dataset: The four XOR examples: inputs (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) with outputs 0, 1, 1, 0. Everything is built from scratch with NumPy.

steps.title: One neuron by hand
steps.explanation: Weighted sum plus bias, then the sigmoid activation squashes it between 0 and 1.
steps.code:
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

# One neuron: weighted sum, then activation.
x = np.array([1.0, 2.0])
w = np.array([0.5, -0.25])
b = 0.1
z = x @ w + b
print(f"z = {z:.2f}, output = {sigmoid(z):.3f}")

steps.title: A network for XOR
steps.explanation: 2 inputs → 4 hidden neurons (tanh) → 1 output (sigmoid). Weights start random; biases start at zero.
steps.code:
# XOR: no single straight line separates it, so we need a hidden layer.
X = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]], dtype=float)
y = np.array([[0], [1], [1], [0]], dtype=float)

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
W1, b1 = rng.normal(0, 1, (2, 4)), np.zeros((1, 4))
W2, b2 = rng.normal(0, 1, (4, 1)), np.zeros((1, 1))

def forward(X):
    h = np.tanh(X @ W1 + b1)          # hidden layer
    out = sigmoid(h @ W2 + b2)        # output layer
    return h, out

steps.title: Train with backpropagation
steps.explanation: Forward pass, mean squared error, then the chain rule gives each weight's gradient. Every step moves the weights a little downhill (learning rate 1.0).
steps.code:
for epoch in range(3001):
    h, out = forward(X)
    loss = np.mean((out - y) ** 2)
    d_out = 2 * (out - y) / len(X) * out * (1 - out)
    d_h = d_out @ W2.T * (1 - h ** 2)
    W2 -= 1.0 * h.T @ d_out
    b2 -= 1.0 * d_out.sum(axis=0, keepdims=True)
    W1 -= 1.0 * X.T @ d_h
    b1 -= 1.0 * d_h.sum(axis=0, keepdims=True)
    if epoch % 1000 == 0:
        print(f"epoch {epoch:>4}  loss {loss:.3f}")

steps.title: Check the predictions
steps.explanation: Outputs close to 0, 1, 1, 0 mean the network learned XOR.
steps.code:
_, out = forward(X)
print("XOR predictions:", out.round(2).ravel().tolist())

questions.question: What does a single neuron compute?
questions.answer: A weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function: a = σ(w·x + b). The weights and bias are learned; the activation adds non-linearity.
questions.interviewer_wants: The formula and the role of weights, bias and activation.

follow_ups.question: What does the bias do?
follow_ups.answer: It shifts the activation's input, letting the neuron fire even when all inputs are zero, like the intercept in a line.

questions.question: What's the difference between the forward pass and backpropagation?
questions.answer: The forward pass computes predictions by passing inputs through the layers. Backpropagation goes the other way: it applies the chain rule from the loss back through the layers to compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. An optimiser then uses those gradients to update the weights.
questions.interviewer_wants: Direction of each pass and that backprop computes gradients, while the optimiser updates.

questions.question: Why do neural networks need non-linear activation functions?
questions.answer: A composition of linear layers is itself linear: W2(W1x + b1) + b2 = Wx + b. So without non-linear activations a deep network is no more expressive than a single linear model and can't learn patterns like XOR. Non-linearities let networks approximate complex functions.
questions.interviewer_wants: The collapse-to-linear argument and an example like XOR.

follow_ups.question: What does the universal approximation theorem say?
follow_ups.answer: A network with one hidden layer and enough neurons can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region to any accuracy; it says nothing about how easy that is to learn.

questions.question: How many parameters does a dense layer from 128 inputs to 64 outputs have?
questions.answer: 128 × 64 weights plus 64 biases = 8,192 + 64 = 8,256 parameters.
questions.interviewer_wants: inputs × outputs + outputs, done quickly.

questions.question: What happens if you initialise all weights to zero?
questions.answer: Every neuron in a layer computes the same output and receives the same gradient, so they stay identical forever (the symmetry problem). Use small random initialisation, for example Xavier/Glorot for tanh or He initialisation for ReLU.
questions.interviewer_wants: Symmetry breaking and named initialisation schemes.

questions.question: Walk through backpropagation for one hidden layer.
questions.answer: Forward: h = f(XW1 + b1), ŷ = g(hW2 + b2), loss L. Backward: compute δ_out = ∂L/∂ŷ ⊙ g′, then ∂L/∂W2 = hᵀδ_out and ∂L/∂b2 = Σδ_out. Propagate: δ_h = δ_out W2ᵀ ⊙ f′, then ∂L/∂W1 = Xᵀδ_h and ∂L/∂b1 = Σδ_h. Each step is the chain rule, reusing values stored in the forward pass.
questions.interviewer_wants: Correct chain-rule ordering, the element-wise activation derivatives, and reuse of forward values.

follow_ups.question: Why is backprop efficient?
follow_ups.answer: It reuses intermediate results, so computing all gradients costs about as much as one forward pass, instead of one pass per weight.

questions.question: Your network's training loss isn't decreasing at all. What do you check?
questions.answer: Overfit a tiny batch first; if that fails, there's a bug. Check the learning rate (too high or too low), weight initialisation, that inputs are normalised, the loss and activation pairing (e.g. sigmoid output with binary cross-entropy), gradients for NaNs or zeros, dead ReLUs, and that labels line up with inputs.
questions.interviewer_wants: A systematic debugging order, starting with overfitting a small batch.

cards.title: Straight lines can't draw faces
cards.body: Stack a hundred linear layers and you still get… a straight line. **Activation functions** add the bends that let networks recognise faces, voices and text.

cards.title: In one line
cards.body: After each weighted sum, an activation squashes or clips the value. That non-linearity is what lets layers learn complex patterns.

cards.title: Meet the line-up
cards.body: The ones you'll be asked about.
bullets: **Sigmoid**: 0 to 1, great for a yes/no probability
**Tanh**: −1 to 1, zero-centred
**ReLU**: max(0, z), the default for hidden layers
**Leaky ReLU / GELU**: ReLU's smoother, never-fully-dead cousins
**Softmax**: turns scores into probabilities that sum to 1

cards.title: The two classics
cards.body: Sigmoid squashes everything into (0, 1). ReLU keeps positives and zeroes out negatives: dirt cheap to compute.

symbols.meaning: the neuron's weighted sum w·x + b

cards.title: The vanishing gradient
cards.body: Sigmoid's slope is at most **0.25**. Backprop multiplies one slope per layer, so 10 layers can shrink the signal by about a million times. Early layers barely learn.

cards.title: Why ReLU won
cards.body: ReLU's slope is exactly 1 for positive inputs, so gradients pass through deep stacks without shrinking. It's also just a max, so it's fast.

cards.title: Which one where?
cards.body: A cheat code for real projects.
bullets: Hidden layers → ReLU (or GELU in transformers)
Binary output → sigmoid
Multi-class output → softmax
Regression output → no activation (linear)

cards.title: Myth vs fact
cards.body: ReLU has one famous failure mode.
cards.myth: ReLU neurons can always recover during training.
cards.fact: If a ReLU neuron's input stays negative, its gradient is 0 and it may never update again: a **dying ReLU**. Leaky ReLU keeps a small slope to prevent this.

cards.title: What interviewers listen for

scenes.title: The missing bend
scenes.narration: Stack as many linear layers as you like and you still get a straight line. Activation functions add a bend after every layer, and those bends are what let neural networks learn real-world patterns.
scenes.on_screen: No activation = still a straight line

scenes.title: Sigmoid and tanh
scenes.narration: Sigmoid squashes any number into the range zero to one, perfect for a probability. Tanh does the same between minus one and one, and it's centred on zero, which often trains a little better in hidden layers.

scenes.title: The vanishing gradient
scenes.narration: Here's the catch. Sigmoid's slope is never more than a quarter. Backpropagation multiplies one slope per layer, so through ten layers the gradient can shrink a million times. The early layers stop learning.

scenes.title: Enter ReLU
scenes.narration: ReLU keeps positive values and zeroes out negatives. Its slope is exactly one when active, so gradients flow through deep networks. It's also just a max, so it's fast. That's why it's the default for hidden layers.

scenes.title: Dying ReLU and friends
scenes.narration: If a ReLU neuron only ever sees negative inputs, it outputs zero, gets zero gradient and can die. Leaky ReLU keeps a small slope for negatives. GELU, a smooth curve, is the favourite inside transformers.

scenes.title: Interview takeaway
scenes.narration: Remember the map: ReLU or GELU in hidden layers, sigmoid for a binary output, softmax for multiple classes, and no activation for regression. Then explain vanishing gradients and dying ReLUs, and you're set.
scenes.on_screen: Hidden: ReLU · Binary: sigmoid · Classes: softmax

python.dataset: Five sample inputs z = −3, −1, 0, 1, 3 and a small vector of class scores for softmax. No dataset needed: we compare the functions directly.

steps.title: Define the activations
steps.explanation: Each is one line of NumPy. GELU uses the common tanh approximation.

steps.title: Compare outputs
steps.explanation: Same inputs, very different shapes: squashing, clipping or smoothing.
steps.code:
z = np.array([-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 3.0])
print("z         ", z.tolist())
print("sigmoid   ", sigmoid(z).round(3).tolist())
print("tanh      ", np.tanh(z).round(3).tolist())
print("relu      ", relu(z).tolist())
print("leaky_relu", leaky_relu(z).round(3).tolist())
print("gelu      ", gelu(z).round(3).tolist())

steps.title: Compare gradients
steps.explanation: σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)) peaks at 0.25; ReLU's slope is 0 or 1.
steps.code:
sigmoid_grad = sigmoid(z) * (1 - sigmoid(z))
relu_grad = (z > 0).astype(float)
print("sigmoid'  ", sigmoid_grad.round(3).tolist())
print("relu'     ", relu_grad.tolist())

steps.title: Watch gradients vanish
steps.explanation: Backprop multiplies one slope per layer. Even sigmoid's best case (0.25) collapses fast.

steps.title: Softmax for the output layer
steps.explanation: Turns raw scores into probabilities that add up to 1.
steps.code:
logits = np.array([2.0, 1.0, 0.1])
softmax = np.exp(logits) / np.exp(logits).sum()
print("softmax   ", softmax.round(3).tolist(), "sum =", round(softmax.sum(), 3))

mistakes: Using sigmoid in every hidden layer of a deep network (vanishing gradients).
Putting ReLU on a regression output, so negative predictions become impossible.
Applying softmax and then a loss that expects raw logits (double softmax).
Computing softmax without subtracting the max, which can overflow.
applications: ReLU/GELU in almost every modern hidden layer
Sigmoid outputs for binary classifiers and gates in LSTMs
Softmax outputs for multi-class classifiers and attention weights

questions.question: What is an activation function and why do we need one?
questions.answer: A non-linear function applied to each neuron's weighted sum. Without it, stacked layers collapse into one linear transformation, so the network couldn't model non-linear patterns. Activations give networks their expressive power.
questions.interviewer_wants: Non-linearity, and the collapse-to-linear argument.

questions.question: Compare sigmoid, tanh and ReLU.
questions.answer: Sigmoid outputs (0, 1), saturates at both ends, max slope 0.25, not zero-centred. Tanh outputs (−1, 1), zero-centred, max slope 1, still saturates. ReLU outputs max(0, z): cheap, no saturation for positives, slope 1 when active, but zero gradient for negatives (dying ReLU).
questions.interviewer_wants: Ranges, saturation, slopes, and one weakness of each.

follow_ups.question: Which would you use in hidden layers today?
follow_ups.answer: ReLU or a variant (Leaky ReLU, GELU) by default; tanh/sigmoid mainly inside gates of recurrent units.

questions.question: What is the derivative of the sigmoid, and why does it matter?
questions.answer: σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)). It peaks at 0.25 when z = 0 and approaches 0 for large |z|. Because backprop multiplies these derivatives layer by layer, deep sigmoid networks suffer vanishing gradients.
questions.interviewer_wants: The formula, its 0.25 maximum, and the link to vanishing gradients.

questions.question: Half the neurons in your ReLU network output 0 for every input. What happened and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: Dying ReLUs: their pre-activations became negative for all inputs (often after a large update from a high learning rate or bad initialisation), so their gradient is 0 and they stop learning. Fixes: lower the learning rate, use He initialisation, switch to Leaky ReLU, PReLU, ELU or GELU, or add batch normalisation.
questions.interviewer_wants: Diagnosis (zero gradient for negatives) plus several fixes.

questions.question: Which activation would you use on the output layer for regression, binary classification and multi-class classification?
questions.answer: Regression: none (linear output). Binary: sigmoid with binary cross-entropy. Multi-class (one label): softmax with categorical cross-entropy. Multi-label: a sigmoid per class.
questions.interviewer_wants: Correct pairing of output activation and loss for each task.

questions.question: Why do transformers often use GELU instead of ReLU?
questions.answer: GELU, x·Φ(x), is smooth and lets small negative values through with small weight instead of cutting them to zero. That gives smoother gradients and has worked better empirically in models like BERT and GPT. Its cost is slightly more computation.
questions.interviewer_wants: Smoothness, non-zero handling of negatives, and that the choice is largely empirical.

questions.question: How do you compute softmax in a numerically stable way?
questions.answer: Subtract the maximum score before exponentiating: softmax(z) = exp(z − max(z)) / Σ exp(z − max(z)). It gives the same result mathematically but avoids overflow for large scores. Frameworks combine softmax with the log in the loss (log-softmax) for the same reason.
questions.interviewer_wants: The max-subtraction trick and why it's equivalent.

takeaways: Activations add the non-linearity that makes depth useful.
Sigmoid/tanh saturate; sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25 → vanishing gradients.
ReLU is the hidden-layer default; watch for dying ReLUs.
Pick the output activation for the task: linear, sigmoid or softmax.

cards.title: Lost on a foggy mountain
cards.body: You can't see the valley, but you can feel the slope under your feet. Step downhill, repeat. That's **gradient descent**, and it's how almost every model learns.

cards.title: In one line
cards.body: Compute the slope of the loss (the gradient), take a small step the opposite way, repeat until the loss stops dropping.

cards.title: The update rule
cards.body: Every weight moves against its gradient, scaled by the learning rate.

cards.title: Step size is everything
cards.body: Tiny steps take forever. Huge steps leap over the valley and bounce up the other side, or even explode. The **learning rate** is the most important knob you'll tune.

cards.title: Batch, stochastic, mini-batch
cards.body: How much data per step?
bullets: **Batch GD**: all data per step, smooth but slow
**SGD**: one example per step, fast but noisy
**Mini-batch**: 32-512 examples, the practical sweet spot

cards.title: Smarter optimizers
cards.body: Upgrades that fix plain gradient descent's weak spots.
bullets: **Momentum**: remembers past steps, rolls through flat parts and zig-zags
**RMSProp**: shrinks steps for weights with consistently big gradients
**Adam**: momentum + per-weight adaptive steps, the go-to default

cards.title: Stretched valleys
cards.body: When the loss is steep one way and flat the other, plain GD zig-zags. Momentum and Adam take a straighter path, reaching the bottom in far fewer steps.

cards.title: Myth vs fact
cards.body: A common overclaim.
cards.fact: Adam usually converges faster with little tuning, but well-tuned SGD with momentum often generalises as well or better, for example in many vision models.

scenes.title: The foggy mountain
scenes.narration: Training a model means finding weights with the lowest loss. Picture standing on a foggy mountain: you can't see the valley, but you can feel the slope. Step downhill, and repeat. That's gradient descent.

scenes.title: The update rule
scenes.narration: The gradient points uphill, so we step the opposite way. Each weight moves by the learning rate times its gradient. Do it again and again, and the loss keeps dropping until it settles at a minimum.

scenes.title: The learning rate
scenes.narration: The learning rate is the step size. Too small and training takes forever. Too big and you leap past the valley, bouncing higher each time until the loss explodes. Tuning it is the first thing to try when training misbehaves.
scenes.on_screen: Too small: slow. Too big: boom.

scenes.title: How much data per step
scenes.narration: Using all the data per step is smooth but slow. One example per step, stochastic gradient descent, is fast but noisy. In practice we use mini-batches of a few dozen to a few hundred examples.

scenes.title: Momentum and Adam
scenes.narration: Momentum keeps a running average of past gradients, so it rolls through flat stretches and damps zig-zags. Adam adds a separate step size for each weight. On a stretched valley, both reach the bottom far sooner than plain gradient descent.
scenes.on_screen: Remember the past, adapt each step

scenes.title: Interview takeaway
scenes.narration: Know the update rule, what a bad learning rate looks like, why we use mini-batches, and what momentum and Adam add. And remember: Adam is a strong default, not a guaranteed winner.

questions.question: Explain gradient descent.
questions.answer: An iterative method to minimise a loss: compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters, then update w ← w − η∇L(w), where η is the learning rate. Repeat until the loss stops decreasing. The gradient points uphill, so moving against it reduces the loss.
questions.interviewer_wants: The update rule, the role of the learning rate, and why the minus sign.

follow_ups.question: Does it always find the global minimum?
follow_ups.answer: Only for convex losses (like linear regression's MSE). Neural network losses are non-convex, so it finds a good local minimum or saddle region, which is usually good enough.

questions.question: What happens if the learning rate is too small or too large?
questions.answer: Too small: training is very slow and may stall on plateaus. Too large: updates overshoot the minimum, the loss oscillates or diverges to infinity/NaN. A learning-rate range test or a schedule (warm-up, decay) helps find a good value.
questions.interviewer_wants: Both failure modes and a practical way to choose the rate.

questions.question: Compare batch, stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent.
questions.answer: Batch uses the whole dataset per update: accurate gradient, smooth progress, but slow and memory-heavy. SGD uses one example: cheap, noisy updates that can escape shallow minima but converge erratically. Mini-batch (e.g. 32-512 examples) balances the two and uses GPUs efficiently; it's the default.
questions.interviewer_wants: Trade-offs in noise, speed and memory, and why mini-batch wins in practice.

questions.question: How does momentum change the update?
questions.answer: It keeps a velocity v ← βv + ∇L(w) and updates w ← w − ηv, with β around 0.9. Consistent gradient directions accumulate speed while oscillating components cancel, so it moves faster along shallow valleys and damps zig-zags.
questions.interviewer_wants: The velocity equations and the intuition of accumulating consistent directions.

questions.question: What does Adam do differently?
questions.answer: Adam tracks a moving average of gradients (first moment, like momentum) and of squared gradients (second moment). Each weight's step is scaled by the first moment divided by the square root of the second, so weights with large or noisy gradients take smaller steps. Bias correction fixes the averages being biased towards zero early on.
questions.interviewer_wants: Both moments, per-parameter adaptive steps, and bias correction.

follow_ups.question: What is AdamW?
follow_ups.answer: Adam with decoupled weight decay: the decay is applied directly to the weights instead of through the gradient, which regularises more correctly with adaptive steps.

questions.question: Your training loss suddenly becomes NaN. What do you check?
questions.answer: Likely exploding values: lower the learning rate, add gradient clipping, check for log(0) or division by zero in the loss, use numerically stable functions (log-softmax), check inputs for NaNs or extreme values, and consider mixed-precision overflow (use loss scaling).
questions.interviewer_wants: Learning rate and gradient explosion first, then numerical stability causes.

questions.question: Why do we use learning-rate schedules like warm-up and cosine decay?
questions.answer: Warm-up starts with a small rate to avoid unstable early updates (Adam's statistics are noisy at first). Decay lowers the rate later so training settles into a minimum instead of bouncing around it. Cosine decay and step decay are common; LLM training typically uses warm-up then cosine decay.
questions.interviewer_wants: Why early and late training need different step sizes.

takeaways: Update: w ← w − η∇L(w); the gradient points uphill.
Learning rate too small = slow, too large = oscillation or divergence.
Mini-batch SGD is the practical default.
Momentum smooths and speeds up; Adam adds per-weight adaptive steps.
